questions.q: What makes a metric a genuine KPI rather than just an interesting number?
options: It's tied directly to a goal the organization has decided matters enough to track and act on
It's any number that can be computed from the data model
It must be a percentage rather than a raw count
It must appear on a card visual specifically
questions.explain: A KPI is narrower than 'any number' — it's a metric explicitly connected to a goal, distinguishing it from numbers that are merely interesting.

questions.q: What test does this lesson recommend before adding a metric to a dashboard?
options: If the number moved significantly, would anyone actually do something differently?
Is the number greater than 1,000?
Can the number be displayed as a percentage?
Does the number update automatically on refresh?
questions.explain: If a significant change wouldn't change anyone's decision, the metric is interesting rather than actionable — it belongs in a detailed report, not the dashboard.

questions.q: Why does Microsoft's guidance recommend keeping a dashboard to a small number of KPIs?
options: A dashboard crowded with many tiles communicates that nothing on it was prioritized, while a shorter list actually gets checked
Power BI technically limits dashboards to five tiles
More tiles always slow down report performance regardless of content
KPI visuals cannot be placed next to other visual types
questions.explain: A dashboard is meant to be an at-a-glance overview — packing it with everything available defeats that purpose, since nothing stands out as prioritized.

questions.q: What does a genuine KPI need beyond just a value?
options: A target, prior period, or benchmark to compare against
A minimum of three decimal places
A unique color assigned to it
It must be calculated using an iterator function
questions.explain: A raw number alone doesn't say whether it's good or bad. A real KPI compares the value against something — which is exactly why the KPI visual from Lesson 55 shows progress toward a goal, not just a number.

questions.q: What should happen to a metric that doesn't have a real target and isn't tied to a decision?
options: It's a candidate for a plain card or a detailed report, not a KPI on the dashboard
It should be deleted from the data model entirely
It should always be converted into a calculated column
It must be hidden using RLS
questions.explain: A metric that fails the KPI checklist still might be useful — just not as a headline KPI. It's better suited to a card, a report page, or a drillthrough.
